title: AI Is Getting Really Good at Messing With Cybercriminals
key_facts: Australian company Apate has spent two years building a system that diverts phone scammers onto calls with AI bots trained to keep them talking without falling for the scam.
Founder and CEO Dali Kaafar says the platform, used by banks and supported by telecom companies, has around 350,000 bots that also join scam chat groups and answer text messages.

Kaafar says Apate calls regularly run more than two hours and the company has collected more than 250,000 pieces of information about fraudsters, from scam URLs to money mule accounts and bank details.
The newsletter tested a demo, found the AI 'victim' responsive and natural, and could not get it to invest in a fake crypto scheme in six minutes.

ETH Zurich researcher Mark Vero says LLM-powered honeypots (decoy systems) kept AI attacking agents busy 'significantly longer' than predictable ones, and the agents flagged them as honeypots at a much lower rate.
WIRED notes scammers still send billions of messages and calls a year and law enforcement has not stopped the growth of digital scamming.
quote_evidence: "What we really like to think is that we're building the perfect victims for scammers," Dali Kaafar, the founder and CEO of Apate, tells us.
In recent research, Vero and colleagues found an LLM-powered honey pot would keep AI agents attacking their system "significantly longer" than a honey pot with more predictable behavior.
Cybercriminals initiate billions of messages and calls each year, with the most sophisticated operations running physical, industrial scale scamming sites.
why_it_matters_hint: AI is being used to waste scammers' time and gather intelligence on them, but the evidence is a company's own figures and a demo.
notes: A weekly newsletter feature; the figures are Apate's founder's claims and the research is an ETH Zurich study described by one researcher.
